for_senior_author: Instrument for an open, unrandomized, placebo-free within-person pharmacokinetic study. Reader 224 notes that METHODS 5.3 ties RoB 2 to randomized trials and to placebo-controlled laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order, while Yanagihara et al. (2003) is open, unrandomized and has no placebo, so ROBINS-I would arguably fit it better; the project's design-to-instrument table maps 'human-laboratory' to RoB 2, so the card follows the tooling and uses the first domain to record the absence of randomization. The same question will recur for every pharmacokinetic card. I have left the instrument as it stands.

Whether cl_ket_brain_imaging_acute should keep the status 'replicated'. The two FDG studies share one laboratory and method, so the independent support is the 2024 meta-analysis, which includes neither of them and whose confidence the editors rate critically low; and four of the nine studies behind its corrected task cluster may be two datasets analysed twice (new reporting issue on sc_ait_bentaleb_2024). The resting-state cluster, which is the one that matches the Zurich direction, is not affected by that overlap, so I have kept 'replicated'; the alternative is 'replicated-same-team' with the meta-analysis named as context.

Whether cl_ket_bioavailability_oral_im should keep 'replicated' now that the statement says the two oral estimates come from different preparations (a solution drunk in orange juice and a swallowed tablet). Two independent groups in the same direction and within three percentage points meets METHODS 6.4 as worded, so I have kept it.

Whether the claim on the other routes should also carry the 2003 paper's own comparison with earlier figures (the Introduction reports approximately 50% nasal and 25% rectal for anaesthesia in children at much larger amounts). It is now a key finding on sc_yanagihara_2003. It would need a new anchor in the claim, and it compares different amounts in a different population, so I have left it off the claim.

Ait Bentaleb et al. (2024) searched the literature in September 2021 and carries a 2024 print year. The gap is now a reporting issue on the card, but the claim does not state it, because no anchor carries the search date and adding one would move the claim off ai-anchored for a second time. If the senior author wants the claim to say when the search closed, an anchor at p. 212 is the place.
